title:
USGOVT101: U.S. Constitution and Politics
Course Introduction
text:
Working definition of government
Government is the organization whose use of organized coercive force is widely treated as legitimate.

title:
USGOVT101: U.S. Constitution and Politics
Course Introduction
text:
Why limit government

Government limits criminal and foreign violence — and is itself coercive force.
Humans are not omniscient. Trade-offs and unintended consequences are normal.
Counter-majoritarian rules exist so losers of elections still have rights and a chance to win next time.

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Today

“Congress shall make no law…” — federal only
Religion clauses: establishment and free exercise
The home as a special zone of protection
What the text does not create: a general right to privacy
A basis for asking: What is missing?

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Why This Matters

By the end of today you will explain why “Congress shall make no law” originally bound only the federal government, how the religion clauses protected both free exercise and state establishments, and why the Bill of Rights treats the home as a special zone of protection without creating a general right to privacy — giving you a basis for asking: What is missing?

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Bridge

Unfinished contract and formal amendments (Lecture 7)
Today: the first great list of limits on federal power
As understood at the Founding — and what changed in the 1940s

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Congress shall make no law…

Large text emphasizing Congress shall make no law

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Federal only

The Bill of Rights originally limited the federal government — not the states

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
As understood at the time

Demand was for restraint on the new national government
Most states already had their own bills or declarations of rights
Barron v. Baltimore (1833): Bill of Rights does not apply to the states
That understanding held until the 1940s (incorporation through the 14th)

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
First Amendment — religion

Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof…

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
No national establishment

No official national church
No automatic membership by birth
No national tax support for churches
No federal payment of clergy salaries

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
It protected state establishments

Timeline of state church establishments and disestablishment

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Free exercise

Practice according to conscience — or not

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Worked with, not against

No establishment and free exercise reinforce each other

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Not in the text

“Separation of church and state” does not appear in the Constitution

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
Second Amendment

A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1
text:
As written

Militia clause explains one reason the right is desirable
The right is held by the people
Disagreement about the explanation does not erase the right of the people

title: Lecture 8: Bill of Rights Part 1

No Soldier shall, in time of peace be quartered in any house, without the consent of the Owner, nor in time of war, but in a manner to be prescribed by law.
